source.title: Bidirectional Transformer Representations of (Spanish) Ambiguous Words in Context: A New Lexical Resource and Empirical Analysis
source.authors: Pamela D. Rivière; A. Beatty-Martínez; Sean Trott

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether model scale predicts performance on human relatedness judgments, using maximum R² rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The scaling-related results are the exploratory comparisons of model size with maximum R² for predicting human relatedness judgments (Sections 5.2 and Appendix A.3.1). Other layer-wise and sense-boundary results do not test the claim versions. Numbers cited from prior work are not treated as study results.
record.test_reason: In exploratory analyses, the study relates parameter count to how well encoder models' embeddings predict human relatedness judgments, in Spanish (12 models) and English (RAW-C). This bears on V6 in a new setting: an embedding-similarity probe, not a standard downstream task. It uses no loss, tokens or compute.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that performance scaled with model size, more clearly in English than in Spanish. They caveat that this was not an ideal scaling test because data and architecture were uncontrolled except within ALBETO, which itself showed no consistent scaling beyond tiny-to-base. In Spanish the effect depended on including sentence-final periods.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares parameter count with maximum R² for predicting human relatedness judgments; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss, training tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that results become a size-performance relationship only when stimuli include periods; RoBERTa models were particularly sensitive to this implementation choice. Model family and multilingual status also corresponded to differences in results.
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2024
record.problems: The scaling analysis is exploratory and compares a limited collection of models with many uncontrolled differences in training data and architecture; only the Spanish ALBETO family was described as carefully controlled. The reported performance is prediction of human relatedness judgments, not held-out pretraining loss. Several model-specific values are shown only in figures, and the authors caution that the English multilingual comparison contains few models.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss is measured.
All: no extrapolation from fitted laws.
All: no controlled shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
All: no other modality or training regime.
Performance as a function of pretraining loss or compute; a fitted predictive law used for prediction; standard downstream task suites; decoder models.

missing.what: Aggregate Spanish result: maximum R² correlated with parameter count across the 12 models (no coefficient stated).
ALBETO family-level result: no clear, consistent scaling beyond the tiny-to-base jump.
The Spanish scaling correlation appears only when stimuli include sentence-final periods; RoBERTa is particularly sensitive.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling result is a small exploratory side analysis of encoder models (5M–355M parameters), with training data confounded across families. The measure is the R² of cosine distance against human ratings, a psycholinguistic probe rather than a standard downstream benchmark, so it is weak evidence for V6. The GPT-4 Turbo appendix uses prompted ratings rather than embeddings and is not a scaling comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether laws fitted on smaller runs predict loss on much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study examines maximum R² for predicting human relatedness judgments from ambiguous-word representations, not a broad suite of downstream tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
It does not fit loss-scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits, or test how those fits vary with counting, schedules, data, or fitting methods.
